about.title: Monterey Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Monterey draws heavy foot traffic year-round, from Fisherman's Wharf to the shops along Lighthouse Avenue and the hotels near Del Monte Avenue, and with that traffic comes uneven walkways, wet floors, poor lighting, and cracked pavement that property owners are supposed to catch. When a business or landlord doesn't, someone gets hurt. California law generally requires an injured person to show the property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn people. That's why what you do in the hours and days after a fall matters: photos of the exact spot, names of witnesses, and a request that any surveillance footage be preserved before it's routinely deleted. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves. We simply connect you with an independent Monterey-area attorney who can evaluate what happened, gather the evidence, and explain your options at no upfront cost.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Your Monterey Fall

items.title: Notice Has to Be Proven
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard before your fall. An attorney knows how to dig up maintenance logs, prior complaints, and inspection records that establish that timeline.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Monterey businesses overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference between having proof and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Cut Both Ways
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, meaning you can still recover even if you're partly at fault, though your share reduces the amount. An attorney will work to keep the blame focused on the property owner's failures, not yours.

items.question: I slipped at a store on Del Monte Avenue but didn't get a copy of the incident report. Is it too late?
items.answer: No, it's not too late. Stores are generally required to keep incident reports, and an attorney can send a formal request to obtain a copy along with any related surveillance video. The sooner this happens, the better the chances the records still exist.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in California?
items.answer: Generally, you have two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit, though claims against a government-owned property, like a public sidewalk or municipal building, have a much shorter window. If your fall happened somewhere that might be publicly owned, it's worth getting a case reviewed quickly.

items.question: What if I was partly to blame for tripping, like not watching where I was walking?
items.answer: California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still recover compensation even if you share some responsibility for the fall. Your total recovery would simply be reduced by your percentage of fault, so it's not an automatic bar to a claim.
